prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BANGALORE, India (CNN) -- Two-year-old Lakshmi Tatma, an Indian toddler born with four arms and four legs, made her first public appearance Tuesday, a week after surgeons in India successfully removed her additional limbs. Doctors said Lakshmi was recovering well as she appeared Tuesday at a news conference. Lakshmi, wearing a plaster cast on her legs to keep her feet up and her legs together to help her wounds heal, was carried into a news conference Tuesday as her doctors announced she was being released from intensive care. "She is coping very well," lead surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil said. "She is being carried around by her mother and her father." Several of her doctors, all of them smiling, described her recovery over the past week "very steady and good progress," one saying she is "out of the woods" as far as serious medical issues are concerned.  Watch the recovering little girl meet the media » . The operation a week ago lasted 27 hours and involved a team of some 30 surgeons, all specialists in pediatrics, neurosurgery, orthopedics, and plastic surgery, working in eight-hour shifts. Lakshmi's extra limbs were part of a conjoined twin which stopped developing in the womb. It had a torso and limbs but no head, and was joined to Lakshmi at the pelvis. Doctors said that without the surgery, Lakshmi would have been unlikely to survive beyond early adolescence. The surgery involved the removal of the extra limbs and the repositioning of Lakshmi's organs. When Lakshmi was born into her poor, rural Indian family, villagers in the remote settlement of Rampur Kodar Katti in the northern state of Bihar believed she was sacred. As news of her birth spread, locals queued for a blessing from the baby. Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, named the girl after the Hindu goddess of wealth who has four arms. However, they were forced to keep her in hiding after they were approached by men offering money in exchange for putting their daughter in a circus. The couple, who earn just $1 a day as casual laborers, wanted her to have the operation but were unable to pay for the rare procedure, which had never before been performed in India. After Patil visited the girl in her village from Narayana Health City hospital in Bangalore, the hospital's foundation agreed to fund the $200,000 operation. Planning for the surgery took a month, Patil said, and Lakshmi spent that month in the hospital. Many villagers, however, remained opposed to surgery and were planning to erect a temple to Lakshmi, whom they still revere as sacred. E-mail to a friend .

BANGALORE, India (CNN) — Lakshmi Tatma, a two-year-old girl from India who was born with four arms and four legs, was seen in public for the first time on Tuesday, one week after Indian surgeons successfully took off her extra limbs.

Medical staff said Lakshmi was healing well when she was presented at a news conference Tuesday. She had a plaster cast on her legs to keep her feet raised and her legs together so her wounds could recover properly. Doctors carried her into the event as they announced that she was being moved out of intensive care.

“She is coping very well,” said Dr. Sharan Patil, the lead surgeon. “She is being carried around by her mother and her father.”

Several of the physicians involved in her care, smiling as they spoke, said her condition had improved consistently during the previous week. One doctor said she was “out of the woods” regarding the most dangerous medical concerns.

The surgery, performed a week earlier, took 27 hours. About 30 surgeons participated, including specialists in pediatrics, neurosurgery, orthopedics, and plastic surgery. They worked in eight-hour shifts.

Lakshmi’s additional arms and legs belonged to a conjoined twin that had failed to fully develop before birth. The twin had a torso and limbs but no head, and it was attached to Lakshmi at the pelvis.

Doctors said that if the operation had not been performed, Lakshmi probably would not have lived past early adolescence. The procedure included removing the extra limbs and moving Lakshmi’s internal organs into proper position.

Lakshmi was born to a poor rural family in India. In the isolated village of Rampur Kodar Katti, in the northern state of Bihar, many residents believed she was holy. After word of her birth spread, people in the area lined up to receive blessings from the infant.

Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, named her after Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth, who is traditionally shown with four arms.

But the family later had to hide the child after men offered them money to place her in a circus. Her parents, who work as casual laborers and earn only about $1 a day, wanted her to undergo surgery but could not afford the uncommon operation, which had never previously been carried out in India.

Dr. Patil, from Narayana Health City hospital in Bangalore, visited Lakshmi in her village. After that, the hospital’s foundation agreed to cover the cost of the surgery, estimated at $200,000.

Patil said preparation for the operation lasted one month, and Lakshmi stayed in the hospital during that time.

Even so, many villagers continued to oppose the surgery. Some were making plans to build a temple dedicated to Lakshmi, whom they still regarded as divine.

In 2007, when Lakshmi was about 2 years old, a team of surgeons in the southern Indian city of Bangalore undertook a marathon operation to separate her from the undeveloped body of a parasitic twin joined to her pelvis. The surgery, performed at Sparsh Hospital under the leadership of orthopedic surgeon Dr. Sharan Patil, lasted more than a day and involved dozens of specialists, including pediatric surgeons, neurosurgeons, anesthesiologists, plastic surgeons and orthopedic doctors.

Doctors described Lakshmi’s condition as one of the rarest forms of conjoined twinning. She had been born joined to a partially formed twin that had stopped developing in the womb. The twin had no head and depended on Lakshmi’s blood supply. Its extra limbs and organs were attached to her lower body, leaving her with eight visible limbs and severe deformities of the spine, pelvis and internal organs.

The operation required surgeons to remove the parasitic twin, reconstruct Lakshmi’s pelvis, reposition internal organs and stabilize her spine and lower body. Doctors said the procedure was necessary not only to improve her mobility but also to save her life. Without intervention, she faced a high risk of infections, pressure sores, organ complications and progressive physical deterioration.

Lakshmi was born in Rampur Kodarkatti, a village in Bihar, one of India’s poorest states. Her parents, Shambhu and Poonam Tatma, were laborers with limited means and little access to advanced medical care. The family said they had been approached by people who wanted to display the child because of her unusual appearance, including offers from traveling shows, but they refused.

Her mother said she wanted Lakshmi to live like any other child. Her father said the religious attention surrounding his daughter was overwhelming, but the family’s priority was treatment.

The child’s name and appearance fed local belief that she was blessed. In Hindu iconography, goddesses are commonly shown with multiple arms, each symbolizing power or divine attributes. In Lakshmi’s village, that resemblance led some residents to regard her as an embodiment of the goddess. But doctors emphasized that her condition was medical, not mystical, and that she needed urgent specialized care.

After the surgery, hospital officials said Lakshmi was stable and responding well. The operation was widely reported in India and abroad, both because of its medical complexity and because of the cultural response to her birth.

Physicians said she would require years of follow-up treatment, including rehabilitation and additional procedures, to help her walk and develop as normally as possible. But they described the initial surgery as a success and said it gave the girl her best chance at survival and independence.

For Lakshmi’s parents, the outcome marked a turning point. The child once worshipped by some villagers as a living goddess had been given the possibility of something her family wanted even more: an ordinary life.

## Lakshmi Tatma: The Indian Girl Born With Eight Limbs

Lakshmi Tatma, a young girl from a poor village in Bihar, India, became internationally known after she was born with eight limbs — four arms and four legs — a rare condition caused by an undeveloped conjoined twin attached to her body. Because of her appearance, she was named after Lakshmi, the Hindu goddess of wealth and prosperity, who is traditionally depicted with multiple arms.

Lakshmi’s condition was the result of a parasitic twin, a form of conjoined twinning in which one twin stops developing in the womb but remains physically attached to the surviving child. In Lakshmi’s case, the extra limbs and organs placed severe strain on her body and threatened her ability to live a normal life.

In 2007, when she was about two years old, Lakshmi underwent a complex operation at Sparsh Hospital in Bangalore. The surgery, reported to have cost around $200,000, was funded by the hospital’s charitable foundation, allowing her family — who could not afford such treatment — to proceed with the life-changing procedure.

The operation involved a large team of surgeons and medical specialists who worked for more than 24 hours to separate the parasitic twin’s body parts, reconstruct Lakshmi’s pelvis, and preserve her organs and limbs. Doctors removed the extra limbs and corrected major skeletal and internal abnormalities.

The surgery was considered a success and gave Lakshmi a far better chance at survival and mobility. Her case drew global attention not only because of its medical rarity, but also because of the cultural symbolism surrounding her name and appearance. Many people in her village had viewed her as a divine child, while doctors emphasized that she was a child with a serious but treatable medical condition.

Lakshmi Tatma’s story became one of the most widely reported pediatric surgical cases in India, highlighting both the possibilities of advanced reconstructive surgery and the role charitable medical foundations can play in providing treatment to families in poverty.
